questions.clue: Aortic dissection is suspected.
questions.priority: Recognize contraindications before giving STAT aspirin.

questions.stem: A client with ACS used cocaine 1 hour ago and is agitated and hypertensive with chest pain. Which medications does the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: A benzodiazepine for agitation
Nitrates for chest pain and hypertension
A pure beta-blocker such as metoprolol
A calcium channel blocker if vasospasm is refractory
No chest pain medication until the cocaine wears off
rationales: The book says to treat agitation, hypertension and pain with benzodiazepines first.
Nitrates are given first along with benzodiazepines.
Pure beta-blockers are avoided with acute cocaine effect because of the risk of unopposed alpha stimulation.
Calcium channel blockers are added if vasospasm is refractory.
The book directs active treatment of pain and hypertension; delaying care is not appropriate.
questions.clue: The ACS is driven by acute cocaine effect.
questions.priority: Choose drugs that treat cocaine-related ACS without unopposed alpha stimulation.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client being discharged after an MI about aspirin therapy. For each client statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs further teaching.
rows: "I will keep taking aspirin indefinitely unless my provider tells me to stop."
"My maintenance dose will be at least 81 mg a day."
"I can keep taking ibuprofen for my knee pain along with the aspirin."
"Aspirin helps keep my platelets from clumping into clots."
"I can stop the aspirin once I finish cardiac rehab."
rationales: The book says aspirin is used indefinitely after an MI unless contraindicated.
The book gives a maintenance dose of at least 81 mg daily.
The book says to discontinue NSAIDs for at least 6 weeks because they increase the risk of myocardial rupture.
Aspirin disables platelet aggregation to prevent clot formation.
Aspirin is continued indefinitely, not stopped after rehab.
questions.clue: Aspirin is lifelong after MI, and NSAIDs raise the risk of rupture.
questions.priority: Evaluate the client's understanding of post-MI aspirin therapy.

questions.stem: A client with an acute MI is resting comfortably with an SpO2 of 96% on room air and no signs of respiratory distress. Which plan regarding oxygen is appropriate?
options: Withhold supplemental oxygen and continue to monitor SpO2
Apply high-flow oxygen, since every client with MI needs it
Apply oxygen and titrate it to keep the SpO2 at 100%
Apply oxygen to keep the SpO2 above 98% at all times
rationales: The book says to avoid supplemental O2 in a client without respiratory distress and to maintain SpO2 above 90%.
Routine oxygen is not recommended without respiratory distress.
The book warns that hyperoxemia can perpetuate oxidative injury after MI.
The target is SpO2 above 90%; pushing higher in a client without distress risks hyperoxemia.
questions.clue: SpO2 is 96% and the client has no respiratory distress.
questions.priority: Avoid unnecessary oxygen that can worsen injury after MI.

questions.stem: Three days after an inferior wall MI, a client suddenly develops a new, loud systolic murmur. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
options: Expected healing of the infarcted inferior wall
Papillary muscle rupture causing mitral valve regurgitation
A new right bundle branch block from LAD involvement
Restenosis of the right coronary artery without valve involvement
rationales: A new loud murmur is not part of expected healing.
The book links inferior MI to papillary muscle rupture, which causes a loud systolic murmur from mitral regurgitation.
RBBB is an ominous sign of anterior (LAD) MI, and it does not cause a murmur.
A loud systolic murmur points to a valve problem, not narrowing of the artery alone.
questions.clue: A new loud systolic murmur has appeared after an inferior MI.
questions.priority: Recognize a mechanical complication of inferior MI.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with stable angina about warning signs. Which client statement indicates the teaching was effective?
options: "Chest pain that starts while I am resting is normal for my type of angina."
"If my troponin test comes back normal, my chest pain cannot be serious."
"Pain at rest, or pain that gets more frequent or intense, needs care right away."
"Pain from exertion should keep going for a while even after I stop and rest."
rationales: Stable angina is exertional pain; pain at rest suggests unstable angina.
The book notes troponin does not rise in unstable angina, yet it is still a precursor to MI.
The book describes unstable angina as pain that may occur at rest and increases in frequency, intensity and duration, and calls it a precursor to MI, so a change in pattern needs prompt care.
Stable angina pain stops when the exertion stops.
questions.clue: Pain at rest or a change in pattern signals unstable angina.
questions.priority: Teach the client to recognize when angina is becoming unstable.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients after PCI. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client whose ST segments have resolved and who is pain free
A client who is anxious about upcoming sheath removal but has stable vital signs
A client asking when the follow-up appointment will be scheduled
A client who had a stent placed yesterday and now reports new crushing chest pain
rationales: ST resolution and pain relief are signs of successful reperfusion.
Anxiety needs attention, but stable vital signs make this client less urgent.
A question about follow-up can wait.
The book calls stent thrombosis a high-alert PCI complication; new chest pain after stenting needs immediate assessment.
questions.clue: New crushing chest pain has started after stenting.
questions.priority: See first the client with a possible high-alert PCI complication.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram of a client with dilated cardiomyopathy shows enlarged ventricles, atrial enlargement and blood stasis. Which complication should the nurse watch for most closely?
options: Clot formation from blood pooling in the enlarged chambers
Rapid, forceful ventricular contraction
Sudden death from asymmetric septal hypertrophy
Preserved contraction with severely stiff ventricles
rationales: Blood stasis in the enlarged chambers of DCM favors clot formation, so the nurse watches for it.
Rapid contraction is a feature of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy belongs to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Stiff ventricles with preserved contraction describe restrictive cardiomyopathy.
questions.clue: Blood stasis is listed among the DCM findings.
questions.priority: Anticipate complications that follow from the type of cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy has been told the prognosis is poor. The client says quietly, "So I may not have much time left." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "Don't think that way; most people with this type live for many decades."
"It sounds like this news is weighing on you. Would you like to talk about what worries you most?"
"Let's focus on your medication schedule instead."
"You should ask your doctor about that, not me."
rationales: The book states many clients with restrictive cardiomyopathy die within 1-2 years, so this is false reassurance.
Acknowledging the feeling and inviting the client to talk supports coping with a poor prognosis.
Changing the subject dismisses the client's concern.
Deflecting the question closes off communication.
questions.clue: The client is reacting to a poor prognosis.
questions.priority: Use therapeutic communication to support a client facing a serious diagnosis.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a history from a client with newly diagnosed cardiomyopathy. For each history finding, indicate whether it is relevant to the cardiomyopathy assessment.
rows: Hemochromatosis diagnosed 5 years ago
Radiation therapy to the chest for cancer
Seasonal hay fever
Myocarditis last year
Tonsillectomy in childhood
rationales: The book lists hemochromatosis among previous diagnoses to ask about.
Exposure to radiation is one of the exposures the book says to question.
Hay fever is not among the conditions the book lists.
Myocarditis is a previous diagnosis the book says to ask about.
A childhood tonsillectomy is not among the listed conditions or exposures.
questions.clue: The book lists specific diagnoses and exposures linked to cardiomyopathy.
questions.priority: Focus the history on known causes of cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: A client with cardiomyopathy is due for a scheduled beta-blocker. The nurse finds a heart rate of 46/min and a BP of 86/52 mm Hg. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Give the dose, since a slow heart rate is the intended effect
Give half the dose and recheck vital signs in 4 hours
Hold the dose and notify the provider of the slow heart rate and low BP
Give the dose with a large glass of water to raise the BP
rationales: Slowing is expected, but this HR and BP are already low and a dose could worsen them.
Changing the dose without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope.
Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and lower BP; giving one to a client who is already bradycardic and hypotensive is unsafe, so hold and report.
Fluids do not offset the drug's effect on an already low HR and BP.
questions.clue: HR 46/min and BP 86/52 mm Hg before a drug that lowers both.
questions.priority: Check HR and BP before a beta-blocker and hold when they are already low.

questions.stem: The nurse on a cardiology unit receives report on four clients with cardiomyopathy. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client with dilated cardiomyopathy who is resting and asking for a menu
A client with restrictive cardiomyopathy who wants to talk with family about the prognosis
A client with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy who has no symptoms and is awaiting discharge teaching
A 20-year-old with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy who has new runs of ventricular tachycardia on the monitor
rationales: A resting client asking for a menu is stable.
This client needs support, but the need is not life-threatening right now.
An asymptomatic client awaiting teaching can be seen later.
The book links HCM to sudden death in young people from ventricular arrhythmias, so new VT is the priority.
questions.clue: New ventricular arrhythmia in a young client with HCM.
questions.priority: See first the client at risk of sudden cardiac death.

questions.stem: A client with cardiomyopathy is started on an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). The client asks how it helps. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: "It blocks the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, easing vessel constriction and fluid retention."
"It blocks calcium from entering your heart and blood vessel muscle cells."
"It inhibits the sodium-potassium pump so your heart contracts more forcefully."
"It mainly widens your veins to reduce the blood returning to your heart."
rationales: The book says ARBs inhibit the RAAS, reducing vasoconstriction and fluid retention.
Blocking calcium influx describes calcium channel blockers such as verapamil.
Inhibiting Na+/K+-ATPase to strengthen contraction describes digoxin.
Mainly dilating veins describes nitrates.
questions.clue: The drug is an ARB.
questions.priority: Explain each cardiomyopathy drug by its mechanism.

questions.stem: A client with left-sided heart failure has crackles and orthopnea and a BP of 98/60 mm Hg. A new prescription reads "0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL IV bolus over 30 minutes." What should the nurse do?
options: Infuse the bolus as prescribed to raise the blood pressure
Hold the bolus and clarify the prescription with the provider
Infuse the bolus faster to correct the blood pressure sooner
Infuse the bolus with the client lying flat to improve venous return
rationales: A large bolus could worsen the pulmonary congestion shown by crackles and orthopnea.
The book cautions to use fluids carefully and avoid a large bolus in left-sided failure, which already causes pulmonary congestion, so the nurse holds and clarifies.
A faster rate adds even more risk of worsening pulmonary edema.
Lying flat would worsen orthopnea, and the bolus itself is the problem.
questions.clue: Crackles and orthopnea show pulmonary congestion from left-sided failure.
questions.priority: Question a large fluid bolus in a client with left-sided heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing clients with heart failure. For each finding, indicate whether it is more typical of left-sided or right-sided heart failure.
rows: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP)
Hepatomegaly with right upper quadrant tenderness
Positive hepatojugular reflux (HJR)
New restlessness and confusion
Tricuspid regurgitation murmur
rationales: Elevated PCWP is listed among the signs of left-sided failure.
RUQ tenderness and hepatomegaly are listed with right-sided failure.
HJR is a sign of right-sided failure.
Restlessness and confusion are listed signs of left-sided failure.
A tricuspid regurgitation murmur is listed with right-sided failure.
questions.clue: "Left = Lungs"; "Right = peripheral edema + JVD" and systemic congestion.
questions.priority: Sort heart failure findings by the side that is failing.

questions.stem: A client with right-sided heart failure is following a prescribed sodium restriction. Which lunch choices show the client understands the diet? Select all that apply.
options: Fresh grilled chicken with steamed vegetables
Canned chicken noodle soup with saltine crackers
Fresh fruit salad
Deli ham sandwich with pickles
Baked potato with unsalted margarine
Frozen pepperoni pizza
rationales: Fresh, unprocessed meat and vegetables are low in sodium.
Canned soup and salted crackers are high in sodium.
Fresh fruit is naturally low in sodium.
Deli meats and pickles are high in sodium.
A plain baked potato with unsalted margarine is a low-sodium choice.
Frozen pizza and cured meats are high in sodium.
questions.clue: The plan for right-sided failure includes sodium restriction.
questions.priority: Evaluate the client's food choices against the sodium restriction.

questions.stem: A client with left-sided heart failure has crackles in both lungs and reports needing to sit up to breathe at night. How should the nurse position the client?
options: Flat in bed with one pillow
In Trendelenburg position
Upright in a high-Fowler's position
Prone with the head of the bed flat
rationales: Lying flat worsens orthopnea.
Head-down positioning increases breathing difficulty in pulmonary congestion.
Orthopnea and pulmonary congestion are features of left-sided failure; sitting upright eases breathing.
A flat, prone position does not relieve orthopnea.
questions.clue: Orthopnea and crackles point to pulmonary congestion.
questions.priority: Position the client to ease breathing in left-sided failure.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the pharmacologic plan for a client with heart failure. Which statements about the prescribed drugs are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Vasodilators such as ACE inhibitors reduce afterload and preload
Furosemide reduces fluid overload
Digoxin lowers contractility so the heart can rest
Beta-blockers such as carvedilol improve heart function and reduce mortality
Dopamine above 10 mcg/kg/min causes renal vasodilation
Digoxin helps control atrial dysrhythmias
rationales: The book says vasodilators (ACEIs, ARBs, nitroglycerin) reduce afterload and preload.
Diuretics such as furosemide reduce fluid overload.
Digoxin increases contractility; it does not lower it.
Beta-blockers improve heart function and reduce mortality.
Above 10 mcg/kg/min, dopamine stimulates alpha receptors and causes vasoconstriction.
The book states digoxin controls atrial dysrhythmias.
questions.clue: Each heart failure drug class has a specific purpose.
questions.priority: Match heart failure drugs to their intended effects.

questions.stem: The daughter of a client with left-sided heart failure tells the nurse, "Dad suddenly seems confused and restless. Is it just his age?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Confusion is common in older adults, so there is really no need to worry."
"He is probably just tired; let's let him sleep it off and see how he does."
"Please try to calm him down for now while I finish giving my medications."
"New confusion can mean his heart failure is worsening. I'll check him now."
rationales: Blaming age dismisses a sign of worsening failure and the daughter's concern.
Letting him sleep delays assessment of a possible decline.
Leaving the family to manage a change in mental status delays care.
Restlessness and confusion are listed signs of left-sided failure; the nurse acknowledges the daughter's concern and assesses right away.
questions.clue: A sudden change in mental status in a client with left-sided failure.
questions.priority: Treat new cognitive change as a possible sign of decline and support the family.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with suspected pulmonary hypertension. Which findings are consistent with this condition? Select all that apply.
options: Hoarseness
Syncope
Jugular venous distention
Bounding peripheral pulses
Cyanosis
Warm, flushed skin with slow heart rate
rationales: The book lists hoarseness in the history of a client with pulmonary hypertension.
Syncope is a listed history finding.
JVD is a listed physical finding.
Bounding pulses are not among the findings the book lists.
Cyanosis is a listed physical finding.
Warm, flushed skin with bradycardia is not a listed finding.
questions.clue: Pulmonary hypertension strains the right heart and impairs oxygenation.
questions.priority: Recognize the history and physical findings of pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse is screening clients for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Which findings are risk factors or associated conditions for PAH? Select all that apply.
options: A parent with PAH
Methamphetamine use
Lactose intolerance
Lupus or another autoimmune disease
A healed wrist fracture
HIV infection
rationales: Family history is a listed risk factor, and idiopathic PAH may be inherited.
The book lists stimulant abuse among the diseases associated with PAH.
Lactose intolerance is not among the risk factors or associated diseases.
Autoimmune diseases are a listed risk factor.
A healed fracture is not linked to PAH in the book.
HIV is a listed associated disease.
questions.clue: The book lists family history, autoimmune disease, HIV and stimulant abuse.
questions.priority: Identify clients at higher risk of PAH.

questions.stem: A client with pulmonary arterial hypertension has several prescribed drugs. For each drug, indicate its main purpose as described in the plan.
rows: Furosemide
Warfarin
Macitentan
Hydrochlorothiazide
rationales: The book lists furosemide as a diuretic that reduces fluid overload and relieves heart strain.
Warfarin is an anticoagulant used to prevent clots and improve circulation.
Macitentan is listed among the PAH-specific drugs that promote selective pulmonary vasodilation.
Hydrochlorothiazide is listed as a diuretic that reduces fluid overload.
questions.clue: Each drug falls in a different class in the PAH plan.
questions.priority: Know why each PAH drug is given.

questions.stem: The nurse has been supporting a client with PAH who becomes anxious during episodes of breathlessness, helping the client minimize stress. Which finding best indicates these interventions are working?
options: The client reports feeling calmer and describes ways to lower stress during the day
The client asks the nurse to stay in the room at all times
The client avoids talking about the illness and changes the subject
The client refuses to get out of bed for fear of becoming short of breath
rationales: The book's psychosocial plan is to monitor anxiety, provide support and minimize stress; calmer feelings and stress-reduction strategies show progress.
Needing constant presence suggests anxiety is still high.
Avoidance suggests the client is not yet coping with the diagnosis.
Fear-driven inactivity shows anxiety is still limiting the client.
questions.clue: The client describes feeling calmer and using stress-reduction strategies.
questions.priority: Evaluate psychosocial care by the client's reported anxiety and coping.

questions.stem: A goal of care for a client with pulmonary hypertension is to reduce cardiac workload. Which nursing action during morning care best supports this goal?
options: Complete bathing, ambulation and the linen change in one session
Spread care activities out with rest periods between them
Encourage brisk walking in the hall before breakfast
Keep the client flat in bed between activities
rationales: Grouping all tasks together increases demand on the strained right heart.
Pacing activity with rest supports the book's goal of reducing cardiac workload and improving oxygenation.
Brisk exertion raises cardiac workload.
Lying flat does not reduce workload and can make breathing harder.
questions.clue: The goal is to reduce cardiac workload.
questions.priority: Pace activity to limit workload in pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with pulmonary hypertension. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client on a stable epoprostenol infusion who is asking about discharge plans
A client scheduled for a V/Q scan later today who is resting comfortably
A client whose inhaled nitric oxide was stopped abruptly and who is more short of breath
A client with mild ankle edema who is taking furosemide as prescribed
rationales: A stable infusion and discharge questions are not urgent.
A scheduled test can wait.
The book says nitric oxide must be tapered slowly to avoid rebound pulmonary hypertension; worsening dyspnea after abrupt stopping is urgent.
Mild edema under treatment is stable.
questions.clue: Nitric oxide was stopped abruptly and breathing is worsening.
questions.priority: See first the client with a likely rebound crisis.

questions.stem: The emergency department nurse is caring for four clients whose BP is at least 180/120 mm Hg. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: BP 184/122 mm Hg with a mild headache and anxiety
BP 182/120 mm Hg with no symptoms, asking for a work note
BP 188/124 mm Hg with mild shortness of breath and an otherwise normal exam
BP 206/126 mm Hg with new slurred speech and weakness on one side
rationales: Headache and anxiety without organ damage fit hypertensive urgency.
No symptoms and no organ damage fit urgency.
The book lists shortness of breath as an urgency symptom when there is no end-organ damage.
New neurologic deficits suggest stroke, a form of brain target organ damage that makes this a hypertensive emergency.
questions.clue: Neurologic deficits signal target organ damage.
questions.priority: See first the client with signs of hypertensive emergency.

questions.stem: A client in hypertensive emergency had a BP of 220/130 mm Hg when an IV nicardipine infusion was started. One hour later, which BP reading best reflects safe progress toward the treatment goal?
options: 118/72 mm Hg
140/86 mm Hg
rationales: A drop to 170/104 mm Hg lowers BP by less than 25%, matching the goal for the first hour.
This is far more than a 25% drop in the first hour.
This is still more than a 25% drop in the first hour.
The book calls for reducing BP rapidly but cautiously; almost no change is not progress.
questions.clue: The starting BP was 220/130 mm Hg.
questions.priority: Lower BP by no more than 25% in the first hour.

questions.stem: A client treated for hypertensive urgency is going home on an oral antihypertensive. For each client statement, indicate whether it shows understanding or needs further teaching.
rows: "My blood pressure will be brought down gradually over a day or two."
"Urgency means my pressure was very high but my organs were not damaged."
"I should get emergency care if I have chest pain, vision changes or confusion."
"Since I didn't need to stay in the hospital, my blood pressure wasn't serious."
"The goal is to get my pressure back to normal within the first hour."
rationales: Urgency is managed with gradual reduction over 24-48 hours using oral agents.
"U" for urgency means uncomplicated: no acute target organ damage.
Chest pain, vision changes and confusion can signal heart, eye and brain damage, which would make it an emergency.
BP of at least 180/120 mm Hg is severely elevated even when managed as an outpatient.
Rapid reduction is not the goal; even in an emergency, BP is lowered by no more than 25% in the first hour.
questions.clue: Urgency is severe hypertension without organ damage, treated gradually.
questions.priority: Evaluate the client's understanding of urgency and when to seek emergency care.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients with inflammatory heart conditions. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with endocarditis who has a temperature of 100.8 F (38.2 C) and splinter hemorrhages
A client with myocarditis whose SBP has been 86 mm Hg for an hour and who has cool, clammy skin and new confusion
A client with pericarditis whose sharp chest pain is worse when lying flat
A client with myocarditis whose admission troponin was elevated
rationales: Fever in the subacute range and splinter hemorrhages are expected IE findings.
SBP below 90 mm Hg for 30 minutes or more with hypoperfusion (cool, clammy skin, altered mental status) meets the book's criteria for cardiogenic shock.
Positional sharp chest pain is an expected pericarditis finding.
The book says troponin is usually elevated in myocarditis.
questions.clue: Hypotension with signs of hypoperfusion in a client with myocarditis.
questions.priority: See first the client who meets criteria for cardiogenic shock.

questions.stem: A young adult is admitted with chest pain, tachycardia and palpitations, and myocarditis is suspected. Which items in the client's medication and exposure history are recognized causes of myocarditis? Select all that apply.
options: Cocaine use
Lithium therapy
A daily vitamin D supplement
Phenothiazine therapy
Occupational lead exposure
Daily sunscreen use
rationales: The book lists cocaine among drug causes of myocarditis.
Lithium is a listed drug cause.
Vitamin D supplements are not a listed cause.
Phenothiazines are a listed drug cause.
Lead is a listed toxin cause.
Sunscreen is not a listed cause.
questions.clue: The book lists specific drugs and toxins that cause myocarditis.
questions.priority: Use the medication and exposure history to find a cause of myocarditis.

questions.stem: The nurse is identifying clients at increased risk for infective endocarditis. Which conditions in a client's history increase the risk? Select all that apply.
options: Prosthetic heart valve
Well-controlled hypothyroidism
Marfan syndrome
Mitral valve prolapse
Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Congenital heart defect
rationales: Prosthetic valves are a listed risk condition.
Hypothyroidism is not among the listed risk conditions.
Marfan syndrome is a listed risk condition.
Mitral valve prolapse is a listed risk condition.
Allergic rhinitis is not a listed risk condition.
Congenital heart defects are a listed risk condition.
questions.clue: Endocarditis usually affects damaged or artificial valves.
questions.priority: Recognize the structural heart conditions that raise endocarditis risk.

questions.stem: A client with acute pericarditis has had extensive testing, and no cause has been found. The client says anxiously, "If they can't find the cause, something must be seriously wrong." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "The doctors must have missed something, so they will order more tests."
"You really shouldn't worry about this; it is nothing serious at all."
"Not knowing is hard. Often no cause is found; that is the most common type."
"It was most likely caused by a heart attack that you did not notice."
rationales: This raises anxiety and is not supported, since idiopathic is the most common type.
False reassurance dismisses the client's feelings.
The book states idiopathic pericarditis (no known cause) is the most common type; acknowledging the worry and giving accurate information eases anxiety.
Guessing at an unconfirmed cause is inaccurate and may increase fear.
questions.clue: The client is anxious because no cause was found.
questions.priority: Address anxiety with empathy and accurate information.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews assessment and diagnostic findings for three clients. For each finding, indicate the condition it most strongly suggests.
rows: Persistent bacteremia on blood cultures
Troponin I above 0.15 ng/mL after a recent viral illness
Friction rub with sharp chest pain that worsens on inspiration
Osler nodes and splinter hemorrhages
AV block with ST-T abnormalities and a history of toxic exposure
rationales: Blood cultures are the key finding for endocarditis, and persistent bacteremia is its abnormal result.
The book lists troponin I above 0.15 ng/mL and a history of viral illness for myocarditis.
Friction rub and sharp chest pain worse on inspiration are pericarditis findings.
Osler nodes and splinter hemorrhages are listed IE assessment findings.
ST-T abnormalities, AV blocks and toxic exposure are listed for myocarditis.
questions.clue: Each condition has a hallmark finding: cultures, troponin or a friction rub.
questions.priority: Link key findings to the right inflammatory condition.

questions.stem: A client with postural hypotension has done leg exercises, worn compression stockings and kept up electrolyte-rich fluids for several weeks but still becomes dizzy on standing. What does the nurse anticipate next?
options: Restricting fluids to reduce venous pooling
Stopping the compression stockings
Starting IV dobutamine for inotropic support
Starting a medication such as midodrine or fludrocortisone
rationales: Hydration is part of first-line care; restricting fluids would worsen symptoms.
Compression is a first-line measure, not something to stop when symptoms persist.
Dobutamine is an inotrope for heart failure, not a treatment for postural hypotension.
The book says medication such as midodrine or fludrocortisone may be started if symptoms persist after non-drug measures.
questions.clue: Symptoms persist despite first-line non-drug measures.
questions.priority: Step up to medication when non-drug measures fail.

questions.stem: A client is hospitalized with myocarditis. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Promote rest and limit exertion
Support oxygenation as prescribed
Encourage brisk daily exercise to build stamina
Manage fluids and track intake and output
Give large IV fluid volumes without monitoring
rationales: Rest is one of the core treatments the book lists for myocarditis.
Oxygenation is a listed core treatment.
Strenuous exercise conflicts with the rest the plan calls for in a weakened heart.
Fluid management is a listed core treatment.
Unmonitored fluids conflict with fluid management and risk heart failure.
questions.clue: Core myocarditis care includes oxygenation, rest and fluid management.
questions.priority: Reduce the demands on an inflamed heart muscle.

questions.stem: A client with myocarditis has prescriptions for an ACE inhibitor, a beta-blocker, a diuretic and digoxin. Which medication does the treatment plan say to use with caution?
options: Digoxin
The ACE inhibitor
The beta-blocker
The diuretic
rationales: The book lists digitalis "with caution" in myocarditis treatment.
ACE inhibitors are listed without a caution.
Beta-blockers are listed without a caution.
Diuretics are listed without a caution.
questions.clue: Only one drug in the myocarditis plan carries a caution.
questions.priority: Recognize which myocarditis drug needs extra caution.

questions.stem: A client with an infected prosthetic heart valve is scheduled for valve replacement surgery. During preoperative preparation, the client cannot explain what the surgery involves and the consent form is unsigned. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain the surgical risks and have the client sign the form
Notify the surgeon so the procedure can be explained before consent is obtained
Have a family member sign, since the surgery is necessary
Continue the preparation, since infected prosthetic valves must be replaced
rationales: Explaining surgical risks to obtain consent is the surgeon's responsibility.
The surgeon who performs the procedure explains it and obtains informed consent; the nurse advocates by notifying the surgeon.
A capable adult client gives their own consent.
Valve replacement is indicated for prosthetic valve infection, but surgery cannot proceed without informed consent.
questions.clue: The client cannot explain the planned surgery.
questions.priority: Ensure informed consent before an indicated procedure.

questions.stem: Endocarditis can be acquired in the hospital. Which nursing action best reduces this risk for a client with a central IV catheter and a prosthetic heart valve?
options: Switch to clean technique once the client is stable
Leave the IV catheter in place as long as possible to avoid new sticks
Use strict aseptic technique when accessing and caring for the IV catheter
Give prophylactic antibiotics before each dressing change
rationales: Clean technique raises the risk of introducing bacteria into the line.
Keeping lines in longer than needed increases infection risk.
The book lists IV catheters and prosthetic valves as sources of nosocomial endocarditis; aseptic line care reduces bacteremia.
The book reserves prophylactic antibiotics for invasive procedures such as dental, GU and GI work, not routine dressing changes.
questions.clue: The client has an IV catheter and a prosthetic valve, both nosocomial sources.
questions.priority: Prevent catheter-related bacteremia in high-risk clients.

questions.stem: A client with pericarditis reports sharp chest pain that worsens when lying flat. Which position should the nurse help the client assume for comfort?
options: Supine with the bed flat
Trendelenburg position
Left side-lying with the bed flat
Sitting up and leaning forward
rationales: Lying flat is the position the book says makes the pain worse.
A head-down position is not a comfort measure for pericarditis.
A flat side-lying position keeps the client recumbent.
Because pericarditis pain worsens lying flat, an upright, forward-leaning position eases it.
questions.clue: The pain worsens when the client lies flat.
questions.priority: Use positioning as a comfort measure for pericarditis pain.

questions.stem: The parents of a 15-year-old admitted with severe myocarditis ask why their child is on continuous cardiac monitoring. They look frightened. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "I can see you are worried. Myocarditis can cause irregular rhythms, so we watch closely."
"Monitoring is just routine for everyone here; there's really nothing to worry about."
"Myocarditis often causes sudden death in young people, so you should prepare yourselves."
"You will need to ask the provider about that; I am not able to discuss it with you."
rationales: The book notes severe myocarditis can cause arrhythmias; acknowledging fear and explaining the purpose of monitoring supports the family.
False reassurance dismisses a real concern.
This is alarming and overstates the risk the book describes for severe cases.
Explaining the purpose of monitoring to a minor's parents is within the nurse's role; deflecting leaves the family without support.
questions.clue: Frightened parents ask why monitoring is needed.
questions.priority: Support the family with empathy and honest information.

questions.stem: A client with pericarditis develops new JVD, and the BP falls from 128/76 to 92/70 mm Hg. Using SBAR, which recommendation should the nurse give the provider?
options: "Please increase the ibuprofen dose, since the client's chest pain is getting worse."
"I'm concerned about tamponade. Please evaluate the client now and consider an echo."
"I recommend that we recheck the blood pressure in 4 hours and call if it drops."
"Please order compression stockings to help raise the client's low blood pressure."
rationales: More NSAID does not address possible tamponade.
The book says to always assess for tamponade in pericarditis; JVD and low BP need prompt evaluation, and echocardiography is a listed test.
Waiting 4 hours delays care for a possible emergency.
Compression stockings treat postural hypotension, not tamponade.
questions.clue: New JVD and a narrowing pulse pressure with falling BP in pericarditis.
questions.priority: Give a clear, urgent SBAR recommendation for suspected tamponade.

questions.stem: A client develops a DVT after 10 days of bed rest following surgery. Which element of Virchow's triad does the prolonged immobility mainly represent?
options: Hypercoagulability
Endothelial injury
Venous stasis
Arterial stenosis
rationales: Hypercoagulability is increased clotting tendency, as with inherited clotting disorders or cancer.
Endothelial injury is damage to the vessel wall, not slowed flow.
Immobility slows venous blood flow, which is stasis, one of the three Virchow's triad elements.
Arterial stenosis causes arterial occlusive disease and is not part of Virchow's triad.
questions.clue: Prolonged bed rest slows blood flow in the leg veins.
questions.priority: Link DVT risk factors to the elements of Virchow's triad.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing clients for risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Which factors increase the risk? Select all that apply.
options: Active cancer
Hyperlipidemia
Pregnancy
Inherited clotting disorder
Recent surgery
Diabetes
rationales: Cancer is a listed risk factor for venous occlusion.
Hyperlipidemia is listed as a risk factor for arterial occlusive disease, not DVT.
Pregnancy is a listed DVT risk factor.
Inherited clotting disorders are a listed DVT risk factor.
Surgery is a listed DVT risk factor.
Diabetes is listed as a risk factor for arterial disease, not DVT.
questions.clue: The book separates arterial and venous risk factors.
questions.priority: Identify clients at risk for venous thrombosis.

questions.stem: A client with peripheral arterial occlusive disease (PAOD) has cool, pale feet and diminished pedal pulses. Which measure is most important to include in daily care?
options: Keep the legs elevated above heart level
Massage the calves firmly to improve circulation
Apply tight compression stockings
Inspect the toes and pressure points for ulcers
rationales: Elevation further reduces arterial flow to an already ischemic limb.
Massage does not relieve arterial narrowing and can injure fragile skin.
Compression stockings are a venous treatment and can further limit arterial flow.
The book lists ulcers on the toes or pressure points as a PAOD finding, so daily skin inspection catches them early.
questions.clue: Reduced arterial supply puts the toes and pressure points at risk of ulcers.
questions.priority: Protect ischemic skin through daily foot inspection.

questions.stem: A client with DVT is going home on warfarin. Which instruction is most important for the client's safety?
options: Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor to reduce bleeding
Double the next dose if a dose is missed
Stop the warfarin once the leg swelling goes away
Take extra doses on days the leg feels more swollen
rationales: Warfarin is an anticoagulant listed for DVT, so bleeding precautions are a safety priority.
Doubling doses increases the risk of bleeding.
Stopping on the client's own judgment risks clot extension; changes are made by the provider.
Self-adjusting the dose increases bleeding risk.
questions.clue: The client will be taking an anticoagulant at home.
questions.priority: Teach bleeding precautions with anticoagulant therapy.

questions.stem: A client with a known DVT suddenly reports shortness of breath. The nurse calls the provider using SBAR. Which statement belongs in the Assessment part of the report?
options: "The client was admitted 3 days ago with a left calf DVT."
"I think the clot may have dislodged and caused a pulmonary embolism."
"Please come see the client now and order the appropriate imaging."
"I'm calling about the client in room 12, who is suddenly short of breath."
rationales: Admission history is Background.
The Assessment gives the nurse's interpretation: the book notes a DVT can cause pulmonary embolism if the thrombus dislodges.
A request for action is the Recommendation.
Identifying the client and the immediate problem is the Situation.
questions.clue: Sudden dyspnea in a client with DVT suggests the clot has moved.
questions.priority: Communicate the nurse's clinical interpretation clearly in SBAR.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews treatment plans for clients with vascular occlusion. For which client is thrombolytic therapy most likely to be part of the plan?
options: A client with a DVT for whom anticoagulation is contraindicated
A client with claudication from PAOD
A client with a severe DVT
A client with an uncomplicated DVT who is responding to heparin
rationales: When anticoagulation is contraindicated, the book lists an IVC filter.
PAOD is treated with antiplatelets, statins, exercise and revascularization, not thrombolytics.
The book lists thrombolytic therapy for venous occlusion in severe cases.
An uncomplicated DVT improving on anticoagulation does not call for thrombolysis.
questions.clue: Thrombolysis is reserved for severe venous occlusion.
questions.priority: Match the DVT treatment to the severity of the case.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a stable client with DVT. For each task, indicate whether it can be delegated to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) or must be done by the nurse.
rows: Apply the prescribed compression stockings
Teach the client about warfarin
Assess the client's new report of shortness of breath
Measure and record vital signs
Evaluate the client's response to heparin
rationales: Applying prescribed compression stockings, a listed DVT treatment, is a routine task for a stable client.
Medication teaching requires the nurse.
New dyspnea may signal pulmonary embolism and needs nursing assessment.
Routine vital signs in a stable client can be delegated.
Evaluating the response to an anticoagulant is a nursing responsibility.
questions.clue: Assessment, teaching and evaluation stay with the nurse.
questions.priority: Delegate routine tasks for a stable client and keep judgment tasks.

questions.stem: A client with a DVT in the right calf asks the nurse to massage the swollen, tender leg. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "A gentle massage will help move the trapped fluid out of your leg."
"I'll massage it for you after your next anticoagulant dose is given."
"A firm massage will help break up the clot so it dissolves faster."
"I won't massage that leg, because rubbing it could loosen the clot."
rationales: Massage can dislodge the clot.
An anticoagulant does not make massage safe.
Massage does not dissolve a clot and risks embolism.
The book warns a DVT can cause pulmonary embolism if the thrombus dislodges, so the leg is not massaged.
questions.clue: The client has a calf DVT.
questions.priority: Prevent embolism by not massaging a leg with DVT.

questions.stem: A client with PAOD and a toe ulcer says, "I just know I'm going to lose my leg like my uncle did." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "That sounds frightening. Most people with PAOD keep their legs; let's talk about protecting yours."
"You're right to expect it; with a toe ulcer, an amputation is very likely now."
"Don't worry about that at all; amputation never happens with PAOD anymore."
"Let's not talk about amputation right now; it will only upset you more."
rationales: The book gives amputation as about 10% of PAOD cases over 10 years, so most clients keep their legs; acknowledging fear and giving accurate, hopeful information supports coping.
This overstates the risk and increases fear.
Amputation is a listed complication, so this is false reassurance.
Avoiding the topic blocks the client from expressing fear.
questions.clue: The client fears amputation.
questions.priority: Respond to fear with empathy and accurate information.

questions.stem: A client with PAOD and claudication has followed an exercise therapy program for 3 months. Which finding best indicates the program is working?
options: The client now has calf pain at rest
The client can walk farther before calf pain starts
The feet are cooler and paler than at baseline
Pedal pulses are weaker than at baseline
rationales: Rest pain is a sign of severe disease, not improvement.
Claudication is pain with walking relieved by rest; walking farther before pain shows better tolerance from exercise therapy, a listed PAOD treatment.
Cooler, paler skin shows worsening arterial supply.
Weaker pulses suggest progression.
questions.clue: Exercise therapy aims to lengthen pain-free walking.
questions.priority: Evaluate exercise therapy by walking distance before claudication.

questions.stem: Several clients have bleeding at a vascular access site after a cardiac procedure. For each anticoagulant, indicate the reversal agent the nurse anticipates.
rows: Warfarin (Coumadin)
Apixaban (Eliquis)
Heparin
Rivaroxaban (Xarelto)
rationales: The book pairs warfarin with vitamin K (phytonadione).
Apixaban is reversed with andexanet alfa.
Heparin is reversed with protamine sulfate.
Rivaroxaban is reversed with andexanet alfa.
questions.clue: Each anticoagulant has a specific reversal agent.
questions.priority: Match the reversal agent to the anticoagulant causing the bleeding.

questions.stem: After a femoral PCI, the nurse finds new swelling and bruising at the access site that is getting larger. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Draw a hemoglobin level
Prepare the client for surgical repair
Apply direct, firm pressure to the site
Obtain a prescription for a reversal agent
rationales: Hemoglobin is monitored, but controlling the bleeding comes first.
Surgery is reserved for bleeding that persists despite other measures.
Direct, firm pressure for at least 20-30 minutes is the immediate bedside action to control access-site bleeding.
Reversal is given "if needed" and takes time to obtain; pressure can be applied right away.
questions.clue: An enlarging hematoma at the access site.
questions.priority: Control active bleeding with direct pressure first.

questions.stem: A client who received a coronary stent is prescribed aspirin plus clopidogrel. Which statement shows the client understands the purpose of these drugs?
options: "These medicines dissolve the plaque inside my arteries."
"They protect my kidneys from the contrast dye."
"I only need them when I have chest pain."
"Taking both keeps my platelets from clumping and forming a clot in my stent."
rationales: Antiplatelets do not dissolve plaque.
Hydration and low-osmolar contrast protect the kidneys, not antiplatelets.
DAPT is taken on schedule to prevent clotting, not only when pain occurs.
The book lists dual antiplatelet therapy to manage stent thrombosis, which is caused by platelet aggregation.
questions.clue: Stent thrombosis is caused by platelet aggregation.
questions.priority: Confirm the client understands why dual antiplatelet therapy matters.

questions.stem: Shortly after a catheter-based valve procedure, a client develops slurred speech and weakness on one side. Which actions does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Immediate neurologic evaluation
A CT scan
Anticoagulation chosen according to the stroke's cause and timing
Starting anticoagulation right away, before any imaging
Rehabilitation therapy as recovery allows
Holding neurologic checks until the client has rested for an hour
rationales: The book lists immediate neuro evaluation for stroke or TIA after a procedure.
A CT scan is part of the immediate management.
The book says anticoagulation is based on stroke etiology and timing.
Anticoagulation depends on the stroke's cause and timing, which imaging helps determine.
Rehabilitation therapy is a listed part of management.
Delaying assessment wastes time in a possible stroke.
questions.clue: Slurred speech and hemiparesis after a procedure suggest embolic stroke.
questions.priority: Act quickly on new neurologic deficits after a cardiac procedure.

questions.stem: After cardiac surgery, the nurse monitors for low cardiac output that would lead the team to start a milrinone or dobutamine infusion. Which findings indicate this problem? Select all that apply.
options: Falling urine output
Cool, clammy extremities
Rising jugular venous pressure
Warm, dry skin with brisk capillary refill
Worsening renal function
Alert and oriented with a stable BP
rationales: Decreased urine output is a listed sign of hypoperfusion from low cardiac output.
Cool, clammy extremities are a listed sign of hypoperfusion.
Rising filling pressures (higher JVP) are listed.
Warm, well-perfused skin argues against hypoperfusion.
Worsening renal function is listed as a trigger for inotropic support.
A clear mental state and stable BP do not suggest low output; obtundation does.
questions.clue: Low CO shows as hypoperfusion and rising filling pressures.
questions.priority: Recognize when low cardiac output calls for an inotrope.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for clients with leg complications after cardiac procedures. For each finding, indicate how the nurse should position the affected limb.
rows: Sudden pain, pallor and no pulse in the left leg
Right calf swelling, warmth and tenderness
Cold, pale foot with no palpable pulse below the access site
Swollen, tender lower leg with a confirmed DVT
rationales: Sudden pain, pallor and pulselessness signal arterial occlusion; the book says keep the limb flat.
Swelling, warmth and tenderness point to DVT; the book says elevate the limb.
A cold, pulseless foot signals arterial occlusion, so the limb stays flat.
A DVT is managed with elevation and anticoagulants.
questions.clue: Arterial and venous occlusion call for opposite positioning.
questions.priority: Position the limb to support arterial inflow or venous return.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a client on the first day after cardiac surgery. Which actions reflect the priority actions for this client? Select all that apply.
options: Assess peripheral perfusion
Encourage deep breathing and coughing
Use clot-prevention measures as prescribed
Keep the client still in bed with the legs immobile
Report early signs of decline promptly
Limit breathing exercises to avoid incision pain
rationales: The book lists assessing perfusion as a priority action.
Promoting breathing is a listed priority action.
Preventing clots is a listed priority action.
Keeping the legs immobile works against clot prevention.
Acting on early signs of decline is a listed priority action.
Limiting breathing exercises conflicts with promoting breathing.
questions.clue: Priority actions: assess perfusion, prevent clots, promote breathing, act on early decline.
questions.priority: Plan postoperative care around the book's priority actions.

questions.stem: Several weeks after valve replacement, a client returns with recurrent angina, a new murmur and worsening heart failure symptoms. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Notify the provider and anticipate an echocardiogram for possible valve failure
Document the findings as part of the expected recovery after valve surgery
Encourage the client to increase activity to build exercise tolerance
Give a PRN analgesic for the angina and reassess at the next shift
rationales: Angina recurrence, new murmurs and HF symptoms are listed signs of graft or valve failure, evaluated by echo.
These findings are not part of expected recovery.
More activity could worsen ischemia and heart failure.
Delaying evaluation risks missing a failing valve.
questions.clue: New murmur, angina and HF symptoms after valve replacement.
questions.priority: Recognize possible valve failure and escalate to the provider.

questions.stem: A client had an embolic stroke during a catheter-based procedure and now has right-sided weakness. The client says, "I'll never be able to take care of myself again." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Stay positive; you'll be back to your normal self in no time at all."
"This is a lot to face. Rehabilitation is part of your plan to regain independence."
"Many people never recover from this, so it's best to plan for long-term care."
"Let's talk about something more cheerful to take your mind off of it."
rationales: Promising full recovery is false reassurance.
Acknowledging the loss and pointing to the rehabilitation therapy in the plan supports realistic hope.
This removes hope and is not based on the client's situation.
Changing the subject dismisses the client's feelings.
questions.clue: The client feels hopeless about a new deficit.
questions.priority: Support coping after stroke with empathy and realistic hope.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients after cardiac intervention. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client receiving prescribed IV hydration before an angiogram scheduled for later today
A client with occasional PVCs on the monitor who has no symptoms and stable vital signs
A client with a growing groin hematoma, a falling hemoglobin and a BP of 88/50 mm Hg
A client who wants to know when the dressing over the access site will be changed
rationales: Hydration before contrast is planned prevention, not an emergency.
Occasional PVCs without symptoms are monitored with ECG.
Swelling, a hemoglobin drop and hypotension are the book's signs of access-site bleeding, which needs immediate action.
A question about dressing care can wait.
questions.clue: Hypotension with a falling hemoglobin and a growing hematoma.
questions.priority: See first the client who is actively bleeding and unstable.

concerns.issue: Pages 58 and 59 are duplicates: both repeat the same 'Acute Venous and Artery Occlusion' comparison table (definition, cause, risk factors, pathophysiology, symptoms) with only a slight layout offset.

S3 description says 'an increased intensity of the ICS can indicate fluid overload'; 'ICS' (intercostal space) appears to be a typo for the S3 sound itself. Heading 'Basic cardiac.' also looks truncated.

Tamponade causes list 'Anticoagulants' twice; Medications box text is garbled ('Support Blood sourcibeeding'); pericardiocentesis box reads 'If absence of myocardial compression', which seems inverted since pericardiocentesis treats compression.

Variant angina box lists 'CCB (Isordil, diltazem)', but Isordil (isosorbide dinitrate) is a nitrate, not a calcium channel blocker, and diltiazem is misspelled. NSTEMI treatment line 'PCI early PCI for high risk patients' is printed twice.

Aspirin STAT is stated only 'for NSTEMI', whereas the page 48 aspirin guidance applies to MI generally; reperfusion arrhythmias are attributed to myocardial 'stunning', which is a different phenomenon (post-ischemic contractile dysfunction).

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes are given as 'often due to hypertension or valvular disease'; HCM is generally described as a primarily genetic/inherited disorder, and hypertension-related LVH is usually distinguished from it. HCM is also equated with HOCM, which is the obstructive subtype.

'Diagnostic Tests' heading is followed by a symptom table (sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, DVT leg swelling) that describes pulmonary embolism rather than cardiomyopathy tests. 'Ask about recent viral or bacterial' is a truncated sentence. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are said to result in low HR, which is not an expected ACEI/ARB effect.

Pulmonary hypertension is defined as pulmonary artery pressure >25 mm Hg without specifying mean pressure; current guidelines (2022 ESC/ERS) use a mean PAP >20 mm Hg. 'Remember: Signs of ventricular failure are evident in systemic circulation' is true only for right-sided failure and conflicts with 'Left = Lungs' on page 51.
States morphine for pain is 'a priority nursing intervention' for MI, while page 48 lists morphine only as an adjunct if NTG is not effective and to avoid in right ventricular MI.

Pericarditis graphic is labeled 'Infected double-walled sac around the heart', yet the same page says idiopathic is the most common cause; the 25-90% idiopathic range is very wide. Endocarditis risk list runs items together ('Previous IE Intravascular devices Skin, bone, GU, GI infections').
Postural hypotension treatment (midodrine, fludrocortisone) and the cardiogenic shock definition appear in the infectious/inflammatory section without connection to its topic; they may be misplaced.

Myocarditis procedures list 'Cardiac transplant or bypass for intractable heart failure'; 'bypass' is ambiguous (coronary bypass is not a myocarditis treatment; mechanical circulatory support may be intended).

'Positive Homan's sign' is listed as a DVT symptom; the sign is spelled Homans' and is generally considered unreliable for diagnosing DVT. Heading says 'Artery Occlusion' while the table of contents uses 'arterial occlusion'.
Post-cardiac intervention complications are numbered 1 (Bleeding, page 60) then 4, 5, 6; the Arrhythmias and Infection boxes on page 61 are unnumbered, so items 2 and 3 are missing labels.

Section numbering is inconsistent: 'B4' through 'B7' labels appear (Cardiomyopathy, Heart Failure, Pulmonary Hypertension, Hypertensive urgency), but there are no B1-B3 labels on earlier sections and later sections are unnumbered; the 'B' prefix also does not match chapter 02.

Diagnostic list says the echocardiogram 'detects right-to-left shunt'; for pulmonary hypertension the echo mainly estimates pulmonary pressures and right-heart function, so this wording seems misleading.

Drug classes are inconsistent: nitrates and calcium channel blockers are listed as PAH vasodilators for all clients, and the endothelin receptor antagonists bosentan/ambrisentan are under 'Vasodilators' while macitentan (also an ERA) is under 'PAH-specific drugs'.
Direct pressure for bleeding is 'at least 20-30 minutes' here but 'at least 20 min' on page 47; consider making the two consistent.
Typo in the Arrhythmias box: 'Myocarrdial irritation'.

Emergent sternotomy box reads 'For myocardicompression' and gives 'Position: HOB 60°, legs elevated', which is unclear and differs from the HOB 30-45° nursing priority on the same page; not used for questions.
'Dobutamine/Dopamine: Boost contractility and renal perfusion' groups the two drugs, but only dopamine has the dopaminergic renal effect described in the dose list; dobutamine's effect is inotropic.
Hypertensive urgency symptoms line is truncated: 'but no end-organ' (missing 'damage').

blueprint: psych has 5 items vs target 6; the chapter's psychosocial content is limited (PAH anxiety support p53, sheath-removal anxiety p47, addiction referral p57), so the remaining slot went to other grounded categories.
blueprint: bcc has 4 items vs target 6 (within tolerance); the chapter's basic-care content is limited to positioning (p45, p51, p62) and non-drug postural hypotension measures (p56).

blueprint (v3): after expansion psych is 12 vs target 13 and bcc 13 vs target 14 (both within tolerance). Psych items rest on the book's anxiety/support (p53), prognosis (p49), cognitive change in left HF (p51), idiopathic cause (p55), myocarditis family support (p54), amputation risk (p60) and stroke rehab (p62); a few bcc items (sodium-restricted meal choices p51, high-Fowler's for orthopnea p51, sitting forward for pericarditis p56) apply basic nursing knowledge to findings the book states.

Bleeding/hematoma management is numbered 1. Reverse anticoagulants, 2. Apply direct pressure, which could be read as an order of actions. cardio-postpci-q10 keys direct pressure as the first bedside action (reversal is 'if needed'); the author may want to clarify the order.

v3 review: 'Risk factors: Family history, pregnancy, and autoimmune diseases' presents pregnancy as a cause of PAH; pregnancy is better described as a high-risk state for clients who already have PAH (it can unmask or worsen it). cardio-pah-q8 no longer keys pregnancy.
